hints: Look closely at the last two stages, a white precipitate forming then dissolving in excess NaOH is a very special clue.
That behaviour tells you the hydroxide formed is amphoteric, so it reacts with both acids and bases to give a soluble complex.
Now work backwards from that amphoteric hydroxide to its oxide and to the element that burns to make a white solid oxide.
walkthrough:
**Spot the Decisive Clue**

Think like a detective and start at the end. A white precipitate that dissolves in an excess of NaOH(aq) to give a colourless solution is the classic test for an amphoteric hydroxide.

Key idea:
$$\text{white precipitate} + \text{excess OH}^- \rightarrow \text{soluble complex ion}$$

**Recall Which Metals Are Amphoteric**

Only a few hydroxides do this at A Level. Aluminium hydroxide is the famous one.

$$\text{Al(OH)}_3(s) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow [\text{Al(OH)}_4]^-(aq)$$
This tells us the solution before must have contained $\text{Al}^{3+}$ ions.

**Check the Earlier Steps Fit Aluminium**

Aluminium burns in oxygen to give a white solid oxide, which then dissolves in acid.

$$4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$$
$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So we get a colourless solution of $\text{AlCl}_3$.

**Complete the Sequence to Confirm**

Adding NaOH first precipitates the hydroxide, then excess dissolves it.

$$\text{Al}^{3+} + 3\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3 \text{ (white precipitate)}$$
$$\text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{OH}^- \text{(excess)} \rightarrow [\text{Al(OH)}_4]^- \text{ (solution)}$$
Every observation matches perfectly, so Y is aluminium.

options.A: Sodium burns to give $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ which dissolves in HCl to give $\text{NaCl}$ solution. Adding NaOH to $\text{Na}^+$ gives no precipitate at all because NaOH is soluble, so it fails at the white precipitate stage.
options.B: Magnesium fits the first three stages: $\text{MgO}$ white solid, $\text{MgCl}_2$ solution, $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ white precipitate. However $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is basic only, not amphoteric, so it does not dissolve in excess NaOH. This is the common trap.
options.C: Aluminium fits all four observations. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is a white solid, dissolves in HCl to $\text{Al}^{3+}$ solution, gives white $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ precipitate with NaOH, which then dissolves in excess to form soluble $[\text{Al(OH)}_4]^-$ because it is amphoteric.
options.D: Phosphorus burns to $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, a white acidic oxide. It dissolves to give an acidic solution, and neutralisation with NaOH gives soluble phosphate ions. No white hydroxide precipitate forms, so it fails the middle stage.
